title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document centralizes Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls and operational workflows across six interdependent areas: RBAC & authentication, audit logging, data residency & retention, secure SDLC, incident response (security), compliance evidence workflows, and risk & exception handling. It is intended for engineering, SRE, product, and security reviewers.

Scope: Applies to all Redwood-managed environments (hosted/production, staging, dedicated control plane, and private customer deployments where Redwood is the control-plane vendor). Customer-specific private deployments may augment these controls as documented in customer-specific runbooks.

1) RBAC & Authentication

Goal: Provide least-privilege access, strong identity assurance, and auditable role changes.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Identity Provider: Okta (primary), with SCIM-managed groups for engineering, ops, SRE, security, product, and sales.
- Access approvals: Access to production/keys/storage requires an approved Jira Access Request ticket and at least one approver from Security or Infrastructure.
- Role owners: Each service or datastore has a named owner in the service catalog (e.g., runtime-api-owner: "eng-serving-runtime-team").

RBAC model and standard roles:
- system-admin: emergency-only privileges; MFA + hardware key required; membership limited to 4 individuals (on-call senior SRE + security lead).
- infra-operator: deploy/build infra (Terraform, KMS rotation); time-bound access via Okta OIDC short-lived sessions.
- developer: non-prod push, can create feature branches and deploy to staging.
- service-account: machine identity (JWT/OAuth2 client credentials).

Authentication and session policies:
- MFA: Enforced for all human accounts (Okta MFA + platform step-up for sensitive operations).
- Password policy: Minimum length 12 (Okta-managed), passwordless encouraged (FIDO2 keys).
- Session TTLs: Console sessions 8 hours; privileged operation tokens 15 minutes; service tokens rotate automatically every 12 hours for ephemeral workloads.

Provisioning and deprovisioning:
1. New hire -> Okta creation via HR sync -> automated group assignment based on role.
2. Access requests for production add -> Jira ticket -> Security review -> time-bound grant via Okta Access Gateway.
3. Offboarding -> HR triggers Okta deprovisioning workflow; all active sessions revoked within 5 minutes.

Periodic controls:
- Quarterly role membership review by role owners.
- Monthly orphaned key/service-account scan (automated) with remediation tickets.

2) Audit Logging

Goal: Capture immutable, tamper-evident audit records for security-relevant events across control plane and customer-facing services.

Log sources and retention:
- Sources: Okta (auth events), AuthZ service (RBAC decisions), API gateway (request/response metadata), serving runtime (model-load, cache-evict), admin console actions, KMS access logs, CI/CD pipeline actions, infrastructure orchestration (Terraform apply).
- Retention baseline: 13 months (production), 3 months (staging/dev). Specific regulated customers may require longer retention; these exceptions are captured in customer SOC agreements.

Log pipeline and integrity:
- Transport: Logs forwarded via rsyslog/Fluentd -> secure Kafka cluster -> immutable S3 buckets with object lock enabled for production.
- Integrity: Daily hash tree generation and cross-account replication; weekly attestation stored in internal evidence store.
- Access: Read access to logs is role-based; write paths are restricted to designated collectors.

Alerting and monitoring:
- Real-time detection: SIEM (Splunk) rules for anomalous access (ex: mass failed MFA, privileged action outside business hours, suspicious service-account usage).
- Escalation: Alerts routed to on-call SRE/security PagerDuty; critical findings trigger incident response playbook (see Section 5).

3) Data Residency & Retention

Goal: Ensure customer data is stored and processed in compliant regions, and retention meets regulatory and contractual commitments.

Residency and processing boundaries:
- Regions: Redwood operates a regional model for customer data: US, EU, and APAC. Customer tenancy configures allowed regions at account creation.
- Cross-region processing: Disallowed for customers with residency restrictions unless an explicit Data Processing Addendum (DPA) permits fallback.

Retention policy (standard):
- Model inputs (raw requests): 30 days default for hosted API, configurable by customer (minimum 0 days, maximum 13 months).
- Audit logs: 13 months production (see Audit Logging).
- User account metadata: 7 years for billing and compliance use cases.
- Backups: Encrypted snapshots retained for 90 days unless customer contract specifies otherwise.

Data deletion and proof-of-deletion:
- Deletion request flow: Customer request -> validation -> asynchronous deletion job -> verification report generated.
- Proof artifact: A signed deletion manifest (object IDs, timestamp, operator id) stored in evidence store.

4) Secure SDLC

Goal: Integrate security controls into development and deployment processes to minimize vulnerabilities in production.

Requirements:
- Threat modeling: Mandatory for all services in scope for production; updated annually or when architectural changes occur. Owners upload models to the threat-models repo.
- SAST/Dependency scanning: PR gate requires passing SAST scan (Bandit/SpotBugs/semgrep) and dependency checks (Snyk/OSS vulnerability) before merge to main.
- Dynamic testing: Quarterly DAST run against staging/post-deploy smoke environments for public endpoints.
- Secrets management: No secrets in code; Vault is the canonical store. CI/CD pipelines fetch ephemeral secrets via short-lived tokens.
- Build/artifact integrity: All production artifacts signed and provenance tracked in the build registry.

Deployment controls:
- Canary deployments with feature flags enabled by default for runtime changes.
- Automated rollback thresholds: If latency SLOs degrade > 15% or error rate increases > 2x for 5 minutes, rollback is triggered automatically (see deployment runbook).

Developer training and attestation:
- Annual secure coding training for engineers.
- New services require security review and checklist sign-off before production access.

5) Incident Response (Security Procedures)

Goal: Rapid detection, containment, eradication, and recovery from security incidents with clear owner and communication flows.

Incident classification and SLAs:
- Sev-1 (data exfiltration, active compromise): Immediate P1 with <15 min acknowledgement by on-call security and SRE, containment within 2 hours, initial customer notification within 24 hours for affected customers.
- Sev-2 (privileged access misuse, significant data exposure): <30 min acknowledgement, containment within 8 hours.
- Sev-3 (non-customer impacting internal issues): <4 hour acknowledgement.

Playbook summary:
1. Detection & Triage: SIEM alert or human report -> Triage channel in #incidents-security -> initial investigation and evidence capture (snapshots, volatile memory capture if appropriate).
2. Containment: Short-term containment (network ACLs, rotate compromised keys, revoke sessions), followed by longer-term mitigations.
3. Eradication: Patch vulnerability, revoke access, validate fix in staging.
4. Recovery: Safe restore process; validate integrity of restored services; monitor for reoccurrence.
5. Post-incident: Postmortem within 7 business days with root cause, timeline, impact, and remediation. Publish anonymized postmortems for internal learning; customer-facing postmortems handled per contract.

Evidence collection & chain-of-custody:
- All evidence (logs, snapshots, hashes) must be ingested into the evidence store with a signed chain-of-custody entry (operator, timestamp, justification).

Communication & notification:
- Internal: Incident channel, daily standups, executive brief on request.
- External: Legal & customer success coordinate customer notifications; security provides technical summary. Regulatory notifications follow statutory timelines for impacted jurisdictions.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Goal: Maintain an auditable, searchable evidence store to support SOC 2, ISO 27001, and customer audit requests.

Evidence types and storage:
- Types: policy attestations, role-review logs, key rotation records, log integrity attestations, deletion manifests, penetration test reports, architecture diagrams, and security training completions.
- Storage: Encrypted S3 bucket with restricted access; artifacts indexed in the compliance catalog (internal UI).

Routine evidence collection:
- Monthly: Role membership attestations, key rotation proofs, patch status summary.
- Quarterly: Pen test summary index, DAST/SAST trend reports, backup verification.
- Annual: SOC 2 control matrix exports, ISO gap-analysis deliverables, completed vendor risk assessments.

Audit response process:
1. Intake: Security receives audit request -> identify control scope -> assign evidence owner.
2. Pack generation: Evidence owner exports artifacts from evidence store into a timebound bundle.
3. Review & redact: Legal reviews bundles for customer-sensitive content; Security approves technical completeness.
4. Delivery: Secure transmission (customer VPN, SFTP, or signed artifact) with temporary access controls.

7) Risk & Exception Handling

Goal: Formalize deviations from baseline controls with documented risk acceptance and compensating controls.

Exception process:
- Request: Service owner files an Exception Request in Jira with rationale, affected control, duration, and compensating controls.
- Review: Security reviews and assigns risk level (Low/Medium/High). High-risk exceptions require CTO approval and quarterly executive review.
- Mitigation & expiration: Exceptions have a hard expiration (max 90 days for Medium, 30 days for High) and automated reminders 14 days before expiry.

Compensating controls examples:
- If MFA cannot be enforced for a legacy system, require IP whitelisting + host-based 2FA + daily attestation logs.
- If log retention cannot meet 13 months due to cost constraints in a specific region, provide hashed snapshots to legal for eDiscovery and quarterly attestation.

8) Ownership, Metrics, and Continuous Improvement

Owners:
- Security: policy, evidence store, exception reviews.
- Eng-SRE: logging pipeline, incident response coordination.
- Eng-Serving-Runtime: runtime-level RBAC and telemetry.
- Product/Legal: customer-facing contracts and DPAs.

Key metrics (examples):
- Mean Time To Detect (MTTD) for security incidents: target < 30 minutes.
- Quarterly role-review completion: 100% of role owners signed.
- Log delivery SLA: 99.9% of audit events ingested into evidence store within 5 minutes.
- Proof-of-deletion SLA: 95% of deletion requests return manifest within 24 hours.

Continuous improvement:
- Quarterly compliance retrospectives with cross-functional stakeholders.
- Rolling threat modeling and annual tabletop exercises (at least two per year).

Appendices

A. Quick RBAC Checklist for Service Owners:
- Define role owners and add to service catalog.
- Ensure service accounts are short-lived and in vault-backed flows.
- Schedule quarterly membership review.

B. Incident Response Contacts (rotate list maintained in runbooks):
- Security on-call: PagerDuty escalation (primary)
- SRE on-call: PagerDuty escalation (primary)

C. Example Evidence Table (textual representation):
| Artifact Type | Owner | Retention | Location |
| Role Review | Security | 3 years | compliance-evidence-bucket |
| Log Integrity Attestation | Eng-SRE | 13 months | immutable-logs-bucket |
| Deletion Manifest | Customer Success | 2 years | compliance-evidence-bucket |

Notes and next steps:
- This document is the canonical control reference for cross-team audits. Owners should keep the linked runbooks and technical configs up to date.
- Planned update: incorporate new Secure Boot attestations for on-prem appliance (planned Q2 2026).
